Hi Maya — thanks again for the discussion this morning. Quick recap and a short list of clarifying questions so Marissa and Camila can size the right config for CartWheel. I attached the template for sample traffic and a preliminary SLO draft (slo-draft-0.2.pdf).

Call recap (what we heard)
- Primary flow: search + assistant where the assistant augments product recommendations.
- Typical request mix: 75% short prompts (50–120 tokens), 25% long prompts (300–600 tokens) including product context.
- You plan to go GA in Q4 with an initial user base that will ramp from a steady baseline to short spikes during marketing drop windows.

Clarifying questions (needed for throughput suggestions)
1) Steady-state QPS (average over 1 hour) vs peak QPS (5–10 minute window) — can you confirm numbers and typical duration of peaks?
2) Tokens per request distribution — median, 90th, and max token sizes. If you can share a sample CSV (timestamp, tokens_in, tokens_out, endpoint) that helps.
3) Streaming usage — which endpoints use streaming? Typical streaming length (seconds) and chunk size?
4) Concurrency expectation from your app (do you expect long-lived connections / websockets that hold concurrency?)
5) Latency SLO targets you care about for short vs long responses (p50/p95/p99).

Proposed next steps
- If you can drop the sample CSV into the HubSpot attachment link (or reply with the file), Marissa will run a quick sizing calc and propose a config.
- Tech deep dive: 30–45m with Marissa + Camila next week to validate streaming behavior and discuss caching/prefix strategies.

If you prefer I can draft an initial sizing note based on what we discussed, but I want to use real samples if possible.

Thanks — Jordan
Jordan Blake

Jordan thanks — great writeup. Answers below and I attached a small anonymized slice of 24h traffic (cartwheel-sample-traffic.csv).

1) QPS: steady-state ~50 QPS (measured as average over 1 hour between 09:00–17:00 PT). We see short marketing-driven peaks up to ~380 QPS that last ~2–5 minutes; occasional sustained peaks ~120 QPS for ~30 minutes during promos.
2) Tokens: median 82 tokens in / ~60 tokens out. 90th ~320 tokens in, max seen ~650 tokens in for long context sessions.
3) Streaming: yes — our assistant API streams the model output to the client for perceived responsiveness. Typical streaming sessions are 1–6 seconds for short replies, up to 10–15s for long multi-paragraph answers. Chunks are small (100–300ms intervals).
4) Concurrency: clients maintain short-lived websockets for streaming; active concurrent connections to the assistant endpoint map roughly 1:1 with request concurrency. Expect concurrency ratio similar to QPS for short responses, but for long responses concurrency can spike because requests are held longer due to streaming.
5) Latency SLOs: for snappy replies we want p50 < 120ms, p95 < 350ms. For long responses we care more about steady throughput and chunking; p95 for first token < 500ms is ideal.

Availability: happy to do the tech deep dive Tue/Wed next week after 11am PT.

-Maya
Maya Patel
VP Engineering, CartWheel Inc

Thanks for the sample, Maya — nice data. I ran a quick pass and wanted to flag a few sizing observations and a recommended approach. High-level takeaways:

- Steady-state 50 QPS with median ~82 tokens in translates to ~4.1k tokens/sec sustained. Peaks (380 QPS * 320 tokens avg during peak) are ~121.6k tokens/sec for short bursts — these will dominate GPU token throughput requirements if unmitigated.

Sizing sketches (very rough):
- For low-latency short replies (p95 < 350ms): prioritize smaller, lower-latency model variants and conservative batching. For your median requests we can aim for ~16–24 concurrent in-flight requests per GPU for a 3B-class quantized model; that maps to ~8–12k tokens/sec effective in steady state depending on batching window.
- For absorbing the 2–5 minute marketing spikes: recommend a burst strategy using autoscaling + reserved capacity mix. Two options:
  1) Provision reserved capacity sized to handle ~60–80 QPS steady + autoscale to handle short spikes.
  2) If cost sensitivity is high, rely more on fallback model variants (smaller family) during spikes and route a % of low-risk traffic to a lower-cost model.

Streaming notes:
- Streaming increases perceived concurrency because connections remain open during generation. If you stream 10s on average that ties up a slot for 10s (vs 200ms for a short reply). To manage this we suggest:
  - Chunked streaming and early first-token optimization (prioritize delivering first token fast).
  - Session-level prefix caching for users who re-request similar contexts (reduces tokens_in workload).
  - Route streaming requests to GPUs with slightly higher memory headroom to avoid preemption.

Next steps for an engineer sizing call
- We need: 24–72h of raw request logs (timestamps, endpoint, tokens_in/tokens_out, user_session_id if available) — the CSV you provided is a great start.
- We'll run a synthetic replay to validate tail behavior and recommend a concrete reserved capacity + autoscale plan.
- Proposed deliverable: sizing note with recommended pool counts (reserved vs burst), model variants and expected monthly tokens cost delta.

I'll draft the first sizing note once we confirm the replay window. Jordan — happy to lead the technical call; Tue/Wed after 11am PT both work for me as well.

-Marissa Cole
Principal Performance Engineer, Redwood Inference
